problem: Find the surface area of the part of the hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that is subject to the constraints ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1$ and $y\ge 0.$

feedback.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the hyperbolic paraboloid $y=1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2},\,(x,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/ab855ef2b9b5363005c14ea37470ed9ecb5853380a301341d20e2cd6095a5d1f.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2})=-2x, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2x)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ u & 1 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
